Personality: Orric Ranufson was a dwarf steeped in tradition from his bones to his beard—his dwarves joked that if a member of the Engineers Guild tried to demonstrate a new wrench in front of him, he would demand proof that the original wrench appeared at least a thousand years ago. He favors "true dwarven weapons" such as axes, crossbows, hammer warriors, and trebuchets, and maintains an indifference that is neither hostile nor contemptuous toward flame cannons, gyrocopters, and any modern device that must be lit with a lead on the battlefield - he believes that these things are the toys of engineers, and that real wars are fought with weapons and battle formations passed down from generation to generation by our ancestors. This traditionalism is not out of stubbornness, or simply stubbornness: Orric once followed an Imperial army against the Orks when he was young, and witnessed the Imperial artillery being completely wiped out because the fuses were damp. After the battle, the Imperial commander knelt in the mud and howled at the piles of scrapped barrels. From that day on, Orric came to a very controversial conclusion among the dwarves: "When your weapon needs to meet more than three weather conditions to function properly, it is not a weapon - it is a wishing machine." His attitude towards non-dwarf merchants is also considered an anomaly among his kind - he opened a "Merchant Hall" in Herne to allow human horse teams to directly enter the city for transactions. This is regarded as an almost shameful concession to humans in traditional dwarf culture, but Orric Rick's response to this is simple: "Every human caravan leaving from Herne has less gold in its pockets and more dwarven steel on its back, which means that the human world outside the mountains will have one more reason to send us reinforcements when the orcs attack their doorstep." He is also an avid player of Herne's horn - every winter solstice, he will personally climb up to the horn cave on the top of the mountain and blow the first trumpet of the year, announcing to all creatures within fifteen miles that Herne is still alive.
Background: Orric is the eldest son of the Drak Zalak clan, a dwarf who was born in the core power circle of the strongest city in the Black Mountains. However, his path to the throne was not smooth: his father, the old king, had a group of loyal supporters among the elders of Herne, but there were also a considerable number of opponents who believed that the old king overly condoned the infiltration of human merchants in Herne. Orric spent eighty years of his adult life serving as a defense officer and trade inspector in the satellite settlements outside Herne - this long "exile" was actually carefully arranged by his father to allow him to accumulate enough knowledge of the human world before taking the throne. His Merchant's Hall system at Herne was conceived during this period. After the death of the old king, the most heated succession debate in Hern's history broke out between the Presbyterians and conservatives who supported the open policy. Orric finally convinced most of the elders with his detailed mastery of border trade data (accurate to every mule cart in every trading season). "The Book of Hatred" is Orric's closest reading - it is not a "reading" to be precise, it is an "action list" - he once ordered the dwarf engineers to dig a collapsed tunnel directly under the path of the undead army during a defensive battle against the undead army of Nehekhara, and buried the entire undead army alive underground together with its Scarab Titan Colossus. This decision was written into the engineering manual as a classic case of "using the terrain itself as a weapon" in the history of dwarf engineering. His most painful memory was of the end times - the Skaven attacked Hern, and the endless swarm of rats overwhelmed the outer defenses. Orric sent the last squad of Hammer Warriors to cover the evacuation of the women and cubs in the city from the secret tunnels, and then personally lit the Horn of Hern and blew it to pieces - until the Horn Cave completely collapsed. He survives, Citadel does not—ultimately, in the new end narrative, this becomes an unfinished ending. In the present day of Karl Franz's time, Orric sat in the Hern Chamber, pressing a rewritten list of hatreds in his hand, and the sound of the trumpet still echoed every day within the fifteen miles.
